title: The Whale That Feeds an Ocean Floor
text: What happens to a whale after it dies? Picture a creature weighing up to two hundred tons, taking its very last breath in the open ocean.
nxt: The answer reveals one of the most astonishing, beautiful, and alien phenomena in all of natural science. And it begins with a long, silent fall into the dark.

title: A Second Life
text: When a whale dies, its journey does not simply come to a quiet end.
nxt: An adult whale carries tens of thousands of kilograms of rich organic matter: blubber, muscle, organs, and a skeleton packed with fat.

title: The Whale Fall
text: The real miracle happens when the carcass does not wash up on a beach, but sinks into the open sea. Marine biologists call this a whale fall.
nxt: Many carcasses float for a while, buoyed by the gases of decomposition. Once those gases escape, or if the whale was lean and dense to begin with, the body sinks.

title: The Deep Desert
text: To understand a whale fall, you must understand the deep seafloor. The abyssal plains cover a huge share of our planet, and much of that ground is a biological desert.
nxt: Sunlight never reaches it, temperatures hover near freezing, and the pressure is crushing. Food is scarce.

nxt: In an instant, a flat, barren landscape has gained a mountain of food.

nxt: These sluggish, ancient-looking predators bite into thick blubber and shake their bodies to tear off chunks of flesh.

title: The Zombie Worm
text: Living among these bacteria is one of the most bizarre animals ever discovered: Osedax, nicknamed the zombie worm, or the bone-eating worm.
nxt: Researchers first found it in 2002, on a gray whale skeleton in Monterey Canyon, off California. These worms have no mouth and no stomach.

nxt: Animals that need something solid to hold on to, such as corals, sponges, anemones, and crinoids, have very few places to settle.

nxt: When it sinks to the deep seafloor, that carbon is carried far from the surface and can stay buried in the deep for a very long time.

title: A Slow Recovery
text: There is a hopeful note, however. Commercial whaling was put on hold by a global moratorium that began in 1986, and some whale populations have been slowly recovering since.
nxt: As their numbers grow, more whales will die naturally and sink, and the deep seafloor may slowly see more of these ancient feasts return.
